Question 2






NoteNote






The Problem
Make a scatterplot of hwy vs. displ using the mpg data frame. Next, map a third, numerical variable to color, then size, then both color and size, then shape. How do these aesthetics behave differently for categorical vs. numerical variables?


The Solution

mpg |> 
    ggplot(aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
    geom_point()







mpg |> 
    ggplot(aes(x = displ, y = hwy, color = cty)) +
    geom_point()







mpg |> 
    ggplot(aes(x = displ, y = hwy, size = displ)) + 
    geom_point()







mpg |> 
    ggplot(aes(x = displ, y = hwy, color = cty, size = displ)) +
    geom_point()









# Raises error due to passing a continous variable to shape
mpg |> 
    ggplot(aes(x = displ, y = hwy, shape = cty)) + 
    geom_point()

When the variable is categorical, all three aesthetics behave simillarly. Each category is assigned a unique color/size/shape.
When the variable is numerical, each of the aesthetics does something different:

color maps each value on a gradient, keeping all information.
size rounds each value to be one of a set of sizes with a positive integer value. It loses some information from the variable.
shape is unable to map to a numerical (continous) variable and raises an error when we attempt to map it.

Question 6






NoteNote






The Problem
Why does the following yield two separate legends? How would you fix it to combine the two legends?

ggplot(
  data = penguins,
  mapping = aes(
    x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm, 
    color = species, shape = species
  )
) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(color = "Species")

Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).











The Solution
Two separate legends appear since our custom name for color is different that the default one for shape. We can fix it by either changing color back to the default legend name or change the name for shape to “Legend”.

ggplot(
  data = penguins,
  mapping = aes(
    x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm, 
    color = species, shape = species 
  )
) +
  geom_point(na.rm = TRUE) +
  labs(color = "Species", shape = "Species")

title: Visualizing Relationships

Question 7






NoteNote






The Problem
Create the two following stacked bar plots. Which question can you answer with the first one? Which question can you answer with the second one?

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = island, fill = species)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill")







ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, fill = island)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill")










The Solution
The first plot (species vs island) shows for each island the proportion of penguins on that particular island. This plot can tell us what the population of each island look like. The second plot (island vs species) shows for each penguin species, the proportion of that species on each island. This plot can tell us the proportion of the total population of each penguin species across the different islands.

Question 6






NoteNote






The Problem
Does it matter what order you used filter() and arrange() if you’re using both?


The Solution
It does matter in terms of computational cost. When you arrange first before you filter, we need to sort a larger number of rows compared to if you filter first. Since sorting has a larger computational cost \(O(n\cdot\log(n))\) (on average using quicksort) than filtering which has a cost of \(O(n)\). Thus we should do filtering first, the operation that is less ‘expensive’.

Question 6






NoteNote






The Problem
For the following data, write a prediction for the output, then check if you were correct, and describe what it does.

# Data Frame
df <- tibble(
  x = 1:5,
  y = c("a", "b", "a", "a", "b"),
  z = c("K", "K", "L", "L", "K")
)

# Part a.
df |> group_by(y)

# Part b.
df |> arrange(y)

# Part c.
df |>
  group_by(y) |>
  summarize(mean_x = mean(x))

# Part d.
df |>
  group_by(y, z) |>
  summarize(mean_x = mean(x))

# Part e.
df |>
  group_by(y, z) |>
  summarize(mean_x = mean(x), .groups = "drop")

# Part f.
df |>
  group_by(y, z) |>
  summarize(mean_x = mean(x))

df |>
  group_by(y, z) |>
  mutate(mean_x = mean(x))



The Solution

a.
The output will be a data frame that starts with all rows that have y = 'a', then will have rows where y = 'b' afterwards.

df |> group_by(y)

# A tibble: 5 × 3
# Groups:   y [2]
      x y     z    
  <int> <chr> <chr>
1     1 a     K    
2     2 b     K    
3     3 a     L    
4     4 a     L    
5     5 b     K    


My prediction was incorrect, group_by() does not alter the order of the rows, it only separates the rows of the data frame into groups.


b.
The output will be a data frame that starts with all rows that have y = 'a', then will have rows where y = 'b' afterwards.

df |> arrange(y)

# A tibble: 5 × 3
      x y     z    
  <int> <chr> <chr>
1     1 a     K    
2     3 a     L    
3     4 a     L    
4     2 b     K    
5     5 b     K    


My prediction was correct, arrange() will change the order of the rows of a data frame. This is different to group_by() since it does create two groups, as seen in the output.


c.
The output will be a table with 2 rows and two columns. The first column will be the unique values of y (‘a’, ‘b’). The second column will contain the average of the x values associated with the values of y.

df |>
  group_by(y) |>
  summarize(mean_x = mean(x))

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  y     mean_x
  <chr>  <dbl>
1 a       2.67
2 b       3.5 


My prediction was correct. The pipeline first groups the data frame by y values, then it takes that new table and takes the average of all x values in each group.


d.
The output will be a table with 3 rows and two columns. The first column will be the unique pairs of y and z values. The second column will contain the average of the x values associated with the (y,z) pairs.

df |>
  group_by(y, z) |>
  summarize(mean_x = mean(x))

`summarise()` has regrouped the output.
ℹ Summaries were computed grouped by y and z.
ℹ Output is grouped by y.
ℹ Use `summarise(.groups = "drop_last")` to silence this message.
ℹ Use `summarise(.by = c(y, z))` for per-operation grouping
  (`?dplyr::dplyr_by`) instead.


# A tibble: 3 × 3
# Groups:   y [2]
  y     z     mean_x
  <chr> <chr>  <dbl>
1 a     K        1  
2 a     L        3.5
3 b     K        3.5


My prediction was correct. The pipeline first groups the data frame by unique (y,z) pairs, then it takes that new table and takes the average of all x values in each group. The message is saying that the data frame that was outputted is no longer grouped by y and z, it is only group by y values. It also says how to hide the message or get the groupings to what it was originally.


e.
The output will contain the same mean_x values as the previous question, but will not have any group and will not have the message before the output.

  group_by(y, z) |>
  summarize(mean_x = mean(x), .groups = "drop")

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  y     z     mean_x
  <chr> <chr>  <dbl>
1 a     K        1  
2 a     L        3.5
3 b     K        3.5


My prediction was correct. The pipeline first groups the rows by unique (y,z) pairs, then calculates the mean of x for each group and ungroups the table. This output is difference since it does not contain any groupings.






f.
The first output will be the same as the output in part e. The second output will be a data frame grouped by (y,z) pairs that adds a new column that contains the mean of the x values in each group, keeping all columns.

  group_by(y, z) |>

Since it keeps all rows from the original table, it output mean_x for every row in each group, instead of only output for each group. Question 2






NoteNote






The Problem
Sketch out the process you would use to calculate the rate for table 2 and table 3. You will need to perform four operations:

Extract the number of TB cases per country per year.
Extract the matching population per country per year.
Divide cases by population, and multiply by 10000.
Store back in the appropriate place.



The Solution
For table1, since cases and population are already separated into their own columns, we can use mutate to calculate the rate.

table1 |> mutate(rate = cases / population * 10000) # Place on right most column

For table2 we first need to “tidy” the table by creating individual columns for the population and cases values. We can do this by filtering by type to obtain a column for just the cases and population respectively, then we can create a new table containing the case and population of each year of each country in its own observation. This will be an identical table to table1, where we can do the same operation.

text:
Question 4






NoteNote






The Problem
Compare the plot below with a plot using a color aesthetic mapping. What are the advantages to using faceting instead of the color aesthetic? What are the disadvantages? How might the balance change if you had a larger dataset?

ggplot(mpg) + 
  geom_point(aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) + 
  facet_wrap(~ cyl, nrow = 2)










The Solution
Some advantages to using facets instead of color mapping include:

More easily seeing the relationship of each group.
If there are many groups, having too many colors may the plot to become unclear.

Some disadvantages include:

Not seeing relationships within the whole dataset.
Some groups may have very few points, which take up space and provides very little information.

With larger datasets, facets become more appealing since facets will more likely have more observations and plotting all observations into a single plot becomes more cluttered and less useful for inference.

The Problem
What is the default geom associated with stat_summary()? How could you rewrite code below to use that geom function instead of the stat function?

ggplot(diamonds) + 
  stat_summary(
    aes(x = cut, y = depth),
    fun.min = min,

The default geom for stat_summary() is "pointrange". To use geom_pointrange() instead of stat_summary, we add stat = "summary".

ggplot(diamonds) + 
  geom_pointrange(
    aes(x = cut, y = depth),
    stat = "summary",
    fun.min = min,
    fun.max = max,
    fun = median
  )

The Problem
What variables does stat_smooth() compute? What arguments control its behaviour.


The Solution
stat_smooth() computes the following:

after_stat(y) or after_stat(x): estimated values
after_stat(ymin) or after_stat(xmin): lower bound of the confidence band
after_stat(ymax) or after_stat(xmax) upper bound of the confidence band
after_stat(se): Standard error of the estimate

The following arguments control its behaviour:

method
formula
n
span
level
method.args
